etymologies.etymologyHTML: Coined by Alfred Nobel in 1867. Ultimately from Ancient Greek δύναμις (dúnamis, “power”) +‎ -ite, most likely under the influence of dynamo or dynamic.

definitions.definition: A class of explosives made from nitroglycerine in an absorbent medium such as kieselguhr, used in mining and blasting.
(figuratively, slang, uncountable) Anything exceptionally dangerous, exciting or wonderful.

quote.citation: 1977 April 30, Steve Sasville, “To Clothe Or Not...”, in Gay Community News, page 6:
quote.text: Even though sometimes I take differing views from some articles and letters in GCN, I think it's a dynamite piece of work. Good luck and thanks again.

quote.citation: 2005, Alex Turner (lyrics and music), “I Bet You Look Good On The Dancefloor”, performed by Arctic Monkeys:
quote.text: And your shoulders are frozen (Cold as the night) / Oh, but you're an explosion (You're dynamite)

That girl was dynamite. Dark hair with killer blue eyes, bronze skin, and an exquisite full-figured body.He warned us: "That issue about what's been happening at that factory, is political dynamite. Keep the lid on it."

definitions.definition: (slang) A strong drug, in particular heroin, cocaine or potent marijuana.
To blow up with dynamite or other high explosive.

quote.citation: 1954 February, Trevor Holloway, “Canada's Transcontinental Railway”, in Railway Magazine, page 128:
quote.text: Gradually the construction gangs cut and dynamited their way through some of the most difficult country in the world.

quote.citation: 1960 February, R. C. Riley, “The London-Birmingham services - Past, Present and Future”, in Trains Illustrated, page 101:
quote.text: [...] on Sunday, August 23, the L.N.W.R. tunnel was closed to enable the old brickwork to be dynamited  away, traffic being diverted meanwhile through the M.R. tunnel.

quote.citation: 2021 July 29, Harry Litman, “Column: Mississippi’s abortion brief dynamites standing law and ‘super duper’ precedents”, in The Los Angeles Times:
quote.text: Even the successful battle in the last century to overturn the court’s infamous Plessy vs. Ferguson “separate but equal” doctrine wasn’t a frontal assault that dynamited precedent.

definitions.definition: (transitive, of brakes) To apply maximum pressure to very quickly.

quote.citation: 2009, Claude M. Pearson, Portia Rising, page 50:
quote.text: Juan dynamited the brakes and the car skidded to a halt.

quote.citation: 2014, Mike Davis, Hunting Men: The Career of an Oregon State Police Detective, page 6:
quote.text: The 1977 Pontiacs had a tendency of dying if you were at high speed and dynamited the brakes.
At the critical moment I'd learned from countless action flicks I dynamited the brakes and felt the impact of the sedan against my rear bumper.

definitions.definition: (intransitive, of brakes) To lock up from being invoked too suddenly.
